questions.prompt: What is computational thinking?
markPoints: Computational thinking is a problem-solving method using computer science techniques, where possible solutions are developed and presented in a way that can be understood by humans and computers
questions.explanation: Model answer: Computational thinking is a problem-solving method using computer science techniques, where possible solutions are developed and presented in a way that can be understood by humans and computers.

questions.prompt: Name the three main approaches used to solve problems related to digital systems.
markPoints: Top-down
bottom-up
modularisation
questions.explanation: Model answer: Top-down, bottom-up and modularisation.

questions.prompt: Describe the top-down approach to problem solving.
markPoints: The top-down approach breaks a complex problem into smaller and smaller problems (modules) until an easily solved problem is defined
the flow of control is always downward, and each level shows a different level of abstraction/detail
questions.explanation: Model answer: The top-down approach breaks a complex problem into smaller and smaller problems (modules) until an easily solved problem is defined; the flow of control is always downward, and each level shows a different level of abstraction/detail.

questions.prompt: How is the top-down approach usually represented?
markPoints: As a tree structure
questions.explanation: Model answer: As a tree structure.

questions.prompt: Describe the bottom-up approach and explain how it differs from the top-down approach.
markPoints: The bottom-up approach is the opposite of top-down: it starts with the smallest module of a problem and combines these modules, moving up a level at a time, until the complete problem is solved (the top-down approach splits a big problem into smaller ones, starting from the abstract problem)
questions.explanation: Model answer: The bottom-up approach is the opposite of top-down: it starts with the smallest module of a problem and combines these modules, moving up a level at a time, until the complete problem is solved (the top-down approach splits a big problem into smaller ones, starting from the abstract problem).

questions.prompt: What is the term for combining modules in the bottom-up approach?
markPoints: Integration
questions.explanation: Model answer: Integration.

questions.prompt: Which type of programming languages is typically associated with the top-down approach, and which with the bottom-up approach?
markPoints: Top-down is typically used with structured/procedural-oriented programming languages (e.g. C)
bottom-up is typically used with object-oriented programming languages (e.g. Python, Java)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Top-down is typically used with structured/procedural-oriented programming languages (e.g. C); bottom-up is typically used with object-oriented programming languages (e.g. Python, Java).

questions.prompt: What is the aim of the modularisation approach?
markPoints: To break a problem into different independent components/modules so a big problem becomes more manageable and solvable
questions.explanation: Model answer: To break a problem into different independent components/modules so a big problem becomes more manageable and solvable.

questions.prompt: Name the four techniques (pillars) of computational thinking.
markPoints: Decomposition
pattern recognition
abstraction
algorithms
questions.explanation: Model answer: Decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms.

questions.prompt: What is decomposition?
markPoints: Decomposition is breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems (modules) that can be understood, developed and tested independently
questions.explanation: Model answer: Decomposition is breaking a complex problem into smaller, more manageable sub-problems (modules) that can be understood, developed and tested independently.

questions.prompt: Explain why the top-down approach uses decomposition.
markPoints: Because the top-down approach breaks the initial problem down until no more decomposition can be carried out, and the resulting sub-problems/modules are then combined (once coded) to solve the initial problem
questions.explanation: Model answer: Because the top-down approach breaks the initial problem down until no more decomposition can be carried out, and the resulting sub-problems/modules are then combined (once coded) to solve the initial problem.

questions.prompt: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using decomposition.
markPoints: Advantage: different people can work on different modules, which can then be integrated (or maintenance can be done at modular level). Disadvantage: sub-problem modules may not combine to solve the initial problem (or: if the problem isn't fully understood, it is difficult to decompose)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Advantage: different people can work on different modules, which can then be integrated (or maintenance can be done at modular level). Disadvantage: sub-problem modules may not combine to solve the initial problem (or: if the problem isn't fully understood, it is difficult to decompose).

questions.prompt: List the four steps of decomposing a problem ready for coding.
markPoints: 1) Identify and describe the problems and processes
2) Break down the problems into separate tasks
3) Describe the tasks and subtasks
4) Communicate (assign tasks/modules to team members to code)
questions.explanation: Model answer: 1) Identify and describe the problems and processes; 2) Break down the problems into separate tasks; 3) Describe the tasks and subtasks; 4) Communicate (assign tasks/modules to team members to code).

questions.prompt: What is pattern recognition, and why is it useful when solving problems?
markPoints: Pattern recognition is identifying common elements/patterns between problems or programs
it helps solve complex problems more efficiently by allowing reuse of existing solutions/modules
questions.explanation: Model answer: Pattern recognition is identifying common elements/patterns between problems or programs; it helps solve complex problems more efficiently by allowing reuse of existing solutions/modules.

questions.prompt: Identify and describe two of the five steps used in identifying and recognising patterns when beginning to code.
markPoints: identifying and interpreting common elements in problems or systems
identifying and interpreting common differences in problems or systems
identifying individual elements in the patterns
describing patterns that have been identified
making predictions based on identified patterns
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two of: identifying and interpreting common elements in problems or systems; identifying and interpreting common differences in problems or systems; identifying individual elements in the patterns; describing patterns that have been identified; making predictions based on identified patterns.

questions.prompt: Give an example of pattern recognition used in a historical or emerging technology context.
markPoints: Example: the Enigma Machine ciphers cracked by Alan Turing and the team at Bletchley Park, where recognising the pattern in each cipher led to deciphering the code (or facial/voice recognition and automated transport, which use predefined/pre-learned patterns)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Example: the Enigma Machine ciphers cracked by Alan Turing and the team at Bletchley Park, where recognising the pattern in each cipher led to deciphering the code (or facial/voice recognition and automated transport, which use predefined/pre-learned patterns).

questions.prompt: What is abstraction?
markPoints: Abstraction is the process of removing or filtering characteristics that are not needed, in order to focus on essential characteristics
questions.explanation: Model answer: Abstraction is the process of removing or filtering characteristics that are not needed, in order to focus on essential characteristics.

questions.prompt: Explain, using the London Underground map example, how abstraction helps solve problems.
markPoints: The Underground map filters out unnecessary detail (actual distances, exact station locations) and keeps only what's needed to plan a journey (lines, stations, interchanges), giving a general model that makes the problem easier to solve
questions.explanation: Model answer: The Underground map filters out unnecessary detail (actual distances, exact station locations) and keeps only what's needed to plan a journey (lines, stations, interchanges), giving a general model that makes the problem easier to solve.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between general and specific detail in abstraction? Give an example using a recipe.
markPoints: General detail is the broad requirement (e.g. "a casserole needs ingredients"), while specific detail is the exact information not required at that level (e.g. exactly which ingredients or quantities)
abstraction keeps the general and filters out the specific
questions.explanation: Model answer: General detail is the broad requirement (e.g. "a casserole needs ingredients"), while specific detail is the exact information not required at that level (e.g. exactly which ingredients or quantities); abstraction keeps the general and filters out the specific.

questions.prompt: What five things should each complete layer of abstraction show?
markPoints: Inputs
outputs
variables
constants
key processes (repeated processes are also listed as something a layer may show)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Inputs, outputs, variables, constants, and key processes (repeated processes are also listed as something a layer may show).

questions.prompt: Define "variable" and "constant" in the context of abstraction.
markPoints: A variable is a value that will change, usually as a result of an input or a calculation
a constant is a value in a program that does not change while the program is running
questions.explanation: Model answer: A variable is a value that will change, usually as a result of an input or a calculation; a constant is a value in a program that does not change while the program is running.

questions.prompt: What is an algorithm, and what four properties must an algorithm have?
markPoints: An algorithm is a plan or well-defined set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem. It must: be clear with clearly defined steps
have clearly defined inputs and outputs
be simple, generic and practical
be language independent
questions.explanation: Model answer: An algorithm is a plan or well-defined set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem. It must: be clear with clearly defined steps; have clearly defined inputs and outputs; be simple, generic and practical; be language independent.

questions.prompt: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using algorithms.
markPoints: Advantage: easy for anyone to understand / breaks the problem into steps making it easier to convert to code. Disadvantage: creating a complete algorithm can be time consuming (or some constructs can be difficult to represent)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Advantage: easy for anyone to understand / breaks the problem into steps making it easier to convert to code. Disadvantage: creating a complete algorithm can be time consuming (or some constructs can be difficult to represent).

questions.prompt: Name the four methods that can be used to represent an algorithm.
markPoints: Flowchart
written description
pseudocode
program code
questions.explanation: Model answer: Flowchart, written description, pseudocode, program code.

questions.prompt: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a flowchart to represent an algorithm.
markPoints: Advantage: the flow of the program can be seen clearly and standardised symbols mean it can be understood by many people. Disadvantage: for a large, complicated program the flowchart can become very large and difficult to follow (changes may require redrawing)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Advantage: the flow of the program can be seen clearly and standardised symbols mean it can be understood by many people. Disadvantage: for a large, complicated program the flowchart can become very large and difficult to follow (changes may require redrawing).

questions.prompt: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using pseudocode.
markPoints: Advantage: can be converted into programming code with minor changes, and is easy to follow even with errors present. Disadvantage: can be as time consuming to write well as the final program code, and it can be difficult to see the logical flow
questions.explanation: Model answer: Advantage: can be converted into programming code with minor changes, and is easy to follow even with errors present. Disadvantage: can be as time consuming to write well as the final program code, and it can be difficult to see the logical flow.

questions.prompt: State one advantage and one disadvantage of using a written description.
markPoints: Advantage: no formal syntax needed, so many people can create one. Disadvantage: temptation to write a complete description, or failure to include every required step
questions.explanation: Model answer: Advantage: no formal syntax needed, so many people can create one. Disadvantage: temptation to write a complete description, or failure to include every required step.

questions.prompt: What is "draft program code" and why might errors be acceptable in it at that stage?
markPoints: Draft program code is program code used to create/develop an algorithm rather than the final solution
errors can be present because it won't be used to run the final program — what matters is that its meaning is clear and can be followed
questions.explanation: Model answer: Draft program code is program code used to create/develop an algorithm rather than the final solution; errors can be present because it won't be used to run the final program — what matters is that its meaning is clear and can be followed.

questions.prompt: What is a trace table used for, and what is meant by "dry running" an algorithm?
markPoints: A trace table is a tool used to dry run (test) an algorithm to make sure no logical errors occur, by recording the values assigned to variables as the algorithm executes
dry running means using sample values for the variables and tracing/running the processing by hand before coding
questions.explanation: Model answer: A trace table is a tool used to dry run (test) an algorithm to make sure no logical errors occur, by recording the values assigned to variables as the algorithm executes; dry running means using sample values for the variables and tracing/running the processing by hand before coding.

questions.prompt: Using the pseudocode below, complete a trace table for NUM = 3 (showing the values of `number` and `output` for each loop iteration).
markPoints: NUM=3: number=1→output 3
number=2→output 6
number=3→output 9
questions.explanation: Model answer: NUM=3: number=1→output 3; number=2→output 6; number=3→output 9.
questions.code:
RECEIVE num FROM (INTEGER) KEYBOARD
FOR number FROM 1 TO 7 DO
    SEND num * number TO DISPLAY
END FOR

questions.prompt: What are "standard algorithms"? Give two examples of standard searching algorithms and two examples of standard sorting algorithms.
markPoints: Standard algorithms are algorithms that follow a recognised
set pattern
commonly used for searching and sorting data. Searching: linear search
binary search. Sorting: bubble sort
merge sort
questions.explanation: Model answer: Standard algorithms are algorithms that follow a recognised, set pattern, commonly used for searching and sorting data. Searching: linear search, binary search. Sorting: bubble sort, merge sort.

questions.prompt: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using pre-written code from a library.
markPoints: Advantage: saves development and testing time because the code is pre-written, tested and optimised. Disadvantage: it may not be exactly what is required, so it needs editing (or it can be difficult to integrate, e.g. mismatched variable names/data types)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Advantage: saves development and testing time because the code is pre-written, tested and optimised. Disadvantage: it may not be exactly what is required, so it needs editing (or it can be difficult to integrate, e.g. mismatched variable names/data types).

questions.prompt: List the six relational operators used in this course and what each one means.
markPoints: = (equal to)
<> (does not equal)
> (greater than)
>= (greater than or equal to)
< (less than)
<= (less than or equal to)
questions.explanation: Model answer: = (equal to), <> (does not equal), > (greater than), >= (greater than or equal to), < (less than), <= (less than or equal to).

questions.prompt: Describe the three logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) used in this course, with an example expression for each.
markPoints: AND: output is true if both conditions are true
e.g. `IF x > 1 AND x < 9`. OR: output is true if any condition is true
e.g. `IF animal = 'dog' OR animal = 'cat'`. NOT: reverses the output of the condition
e.g. `WHILE NOT x`
questions.explanation: Model answer: AND: output is true if both conditions are true, e.g. `IF x > 1 AND x < 9`. OR: output is true if any condition is true, e.g. `IF animal = 'dog' OR animal = 'cat'`. NOT: reverses the output of the condition, e.g. `WHILE NOT x`.

questions.prompt: Explain what the exponent, modulo and integer division arithmetic expressions do, giving an example of each.
markPoints: Exponent (^) raises a number to a power, e.g. 3^3 = 3*3*3 = 27. Modulo (MOD/%) gives the remainder after division, e.g. 50 MOD 8 = 2. Integer division (DIV or /) divides and discards the remainder, e.g. 50 DIV 8 = 6
questions.explanation: Model answer: Exponent (^) raises a number to a power, e.g. 3^3 = 3*3*3 = 27. Modulo (MOD/%) gives the remainder after division, e.g. 50 MOD 8 = 2. Integer division (DIV or /) divides and discards the remainder, e.g. 50 DIV 8 = 6.

questions.prompt: Which pseudocode constructs represent iteration and selection? Give the pseudocode syntax for each.
markPoints: Iteration is represented by `REPEAT <command> UNTIL <expression>`; selection is represented by `IF <expression> THEN <command> END IF`
questions.explanation: Model answer: Iteration is represented by `REPEAT <command> UNTIL <expression>`; selection is represented by `IF <expression> THEN <command> END IF`.

questions.prompt: Give two real-world examples (other than searching/sorting) of where algorithms are used to make decisions.
markPoints: deciding whether a credit card application is approved (and the credit limit/interest rate)
providing personalised recommendations based on previous purchases/viewing
adjusting book/product prices based on sales levels
deciding where to locate a new hospital or emergency service hub
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two of: deciding whether a credit card application is approved (and the credit limit/interest rate); providing personalised recommendations based on previous purchases/viewing; adjusting book/product prices based on sales levels; deciding where to locate a new hospital or emergency service hub.

questions.prompt: Write pseudocode (or describe the flowchart) to validate a password that must be ten or more characters long and include at least one number.
markPoints: Example pseudocode: `RECEIVE password FROM (STRING) KEYBOARD` then check `IF LENGTH(password) >= 10 AND password CONTAINS a number THEN` accept it, `ELSE` display an error message and ask the user to edit the password (exact syntax will vary, but must check length ≥10 characters and presence of at least one number, with an error message and re-entry if invalid)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Example pseudocode: `RECEIVE password FROM (STRING) KEYBOARD` then check `IF LENGTH(password) >= 10 AND password CONTAINS a number THEN` accept it, `ELSE` display an error message and ask the user to edit the password (exact syntax will vary, but must check length ≥10 characters and presence of at least one number, with an error message and re-entry if invalid).

questions.prompt: Name the five main data types used in programming.
markPoints: Boolean
character
integer
real/float
string
questions.explanation: Model answer: Boolean, character, integer, real/float, string.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the term "immutable" in relation to Python number data types?
markPoints: Immutable means that when the value of a number data type is changed, a new object is created (the original object is not modified in place)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Immutable means that when the value of a number data type is changed, a new object is created (the original object is not modified in place).

questions.prompt: Why does the character data type not have its own Python notation?
markPoints: Because a single character would, in Python, actually be represented as a string of length 1 — there is no separate character notation
questions.explanation: Model answer: Because a single character would, in Python, actually be represented as a string of length 1 — there is no separate character notation.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the `int()`, `float()` and `str()` casting functions, and give the output of `int(5.7)`.
markPoints: `int()` returns an integer (from an int, float by removing decimals, or a whole-number string); `float()` returns a float (from an int, float or numeric string); `str()` returns a string representation of a variety of data types. `int(5.7)` returns `5`
questions.explanation: Model answer: `int()` returns an integer (from an int, float by removing decimals, or a whole-number string); `float()` returns a float (from an int, float or numeric string); `str()` returns a string representation of a variety of data types. `int(5.7)` returns `5`.

questions.prompt: Why should a telephone number be stored as a string data type rather than an integer?
markPoints: Because storing it as an integer would remove any leading zero, corrupting the number
questions.explanation: Model answer: Because storing it as an integer would remove any leading zero, corrupting the number.

questions.prompt: Define the term "data structure" and name two examples.
markPoints: A data structure is a collection of data objects that facilitates storing and managing data in a program
examples include lists, arrays and dictionaries
questions.explanation: Model answer: A data structure is a collection of data objects that facilitates storing and managing data in a program; examples include lists, arrays and dictionaries.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a list and an array in Python.
markPoints: A list can contain mixed data types and its items can be edited/removed/added (changeable)
an array contains groups of elements that are all the same data type, commonly used for organising data that will be searched/sorted
questions.explanation: Model answer: A list can contain mixed data types and its items can be edited/removed/added (changeable); an array contains groups of elements that are all the same data type, commonly used for organising data that will be searched/sorted.

questions.prompt: What is a dictionary data structure, and why might looping over one return items in a random order?
markPoints: A dictionary is a general-purpose data structure that maps a set of keys to associated values
it is unordered, so looping over it does not guarantee any particular order of items
questions.explanation: Model answer: A dictionary is a general-purpose data structure that maps a set of keys to associated values; it is unordered, so looping over it does not guarantee any particular order of items.

questions.prompt: State one advantage of using data structures.
markPoints: It optimises memory usage (e.g. lists/arrays can be linked when size is uncertain and memory released when not needed), or it enables data structures to be reused and compiled into libraries
questions.explanation: Model answer: It optimises memory usage (e.g. lists/arrays can be linked when size is uncertain and memory released when not needed), or it enables data structures to be reused and compiled into libraries.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a local variable and a global variable, including where each must be declared.
markPoints: A local variable is only accessible within the subroutine/block where it is declared
a global variable is accessible anywhere in the program, must remain in memory the whole time the program runs, and must be declared at the start of the program
questions.explanation: Model answer: A local variable is only accessible within the subroutine/block where it is declared; a global variable is accessible anywhere in the program, must remain in memory the whole time the program runs, and must be declared at the start of the program.

questions.prompt: Identify the four multiword variable-naming conventions (snakecase, camelcase, pascalcase, Hungarian notation) and give one example of each.
markPoints: Snakecase separates words with underscores (Variable_a)
camelcase capitalises each word except the first (variableA)
Pascalcase capitalises every word including the first (VariableA)
Hungarian notation prefixes the name with the variable's type/purpose using Camelcase (e.g. arrEmployeePayslips)
questions.explanation: Model answer: Snakecase separates words with underscores (Variable_a); camelcase capitalises each word except the first (variableA); Pascalcase capitalises every word including the first (VariableA); Hungarian notation prefixes the name with the variable's type/purpose using Camelcase (e.g. arrEmployeePayslips).

questions.prompt: Why should single-letter variable names I, O and l be avoided?
markPoints: Because they can be mistaken for the numbers 1 or 0
questions.explanation: Model answer: Because they can be mistaken for the numbers 1 or 0.

questions.prompt: What is the Python notation for the integer division (DIV) operator, and what does it do?
markPoints: `//`; it performs division and discards the remainder
questions.explanation: Model answer: `//`; it performs division and discards the remainder.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the Modulus (MOD) operator?
markPoints: It divides the left value by the right value and returns the remainder
questions.explanation: Model answer: It divides the left value by the right value and returns the remainder.

questions.prompt: Given x = 31 and y = 15, what is the result of `x // y` and `x % y`?
questions.explanation: Model answer: `x // y` = 2, `x % y` = 1.

questions.prompt: Given x = 35 and y = 25, evaluate: `x == y`, `x != y`, `x > y`.
markPoints: `x == y` is False, `x != y` is True, `x > y` is True
questions.explanation: Model answer: `x == y` is False, `x != y` is True, `x > y` is True.

questions.prompt: Name the three Boolean (logical) operators.
markPoints: AND
OR
NOT
questions.explanation: Model answer: AND, OR, NOT.

questions.prompt: Given x = 25, what is the output of `print(x > 15 and x < 30)`, and of `print(not (x>15 and x<20))`?
markPoints: `print(x > 15 and x < 30)` gives `True`; `print(not (x>15 and x<20))` gives `True` (x>15 is True, x<20 is False, so the AND is False, and `not False` is True)
questions.explanation: Model answer: `print(x > 15 and x < 30)` gives `True`; `print(not (x>15 and x<20))` gives `True` (x>15 is True, x<20 is False, so the AND is False, and `not False` is True).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the `not` Boolean operator?
markPoints: It reverses (negates) the output of the condition it is applied to
questions.explanation: Model answer: It reverses (negates) the output of the condition it is applied to.

questions.prompt: What Python notation is used to declare a text file and a binary file?
markPoints: `"t"` for text (the default) and `"b"` for binary
questions.explanation: Model answer: `"t"` for text (the default) and `"b"` for binary.

questions.prompt: List the four modes (methods) of opening a file in Python, their parameters, and which ones create a new file if it doesn't already exist.
markPoints: Append ("a") – edits/appends, creates file if it doesn't exist
Create ("x") – creates a file, errors if it exists
Read ("r") – default, errors if file doesn't exist
Write ("w") – opens for writing, creates file if it doesn't exist. Append and Write both create a new file if it does not already exist
questions.explanation: Model answer: Append ("a") – edits/appends, creates file if it doesn't exist; Create ("x") – creates a file, errors if it exists; Read ("r") – default, errors if file doesn't exist; Write ("w") – opens for writing, creates file if it doesn't exist. Append and Write both create a new file if it does not already exist.

questions.prompt: Write the Python code to open and read the first 12 characters of a file called "TestYourself.txt".
markPoints: `h = open("TestYourself.txt", "r")` then `print(h.read(12))`
questions.explanation: Model answer: `h = open("TestYourself.txt", "r")` then `print(h.read(12))`.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between writing to a file (mode "w") and appending to a file (mode "a") in Python?
markPoints: Appending ("a") adds new content to the end of the existing file
writing ("w") overwrites/replaces the entire existing contents of the file
questions.explanation: Model answer: Appending ("a") adds new content to the end of the existing file; writing ("w") overwrites/replaces the entire existing contents of the file.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to close a file after writing to or appending it?
markPoints: If the file is not closed after writing/appending, changes may not be saved and the file will not be up to date
questions.explanation: Model answer: If the file is not closed after writing/appending, changes may not be saved and the file will not be up to date.

questions.prompt: Write the Python code to append the text "This is question 4" to a file named "TestYourself.txt".
markPoints: `h = open("TestYourself.txt", "a")` then `h.write("This is question 4")` then `h.close()`
questions.explanation: Model answer: `h = open("TestYourself.txt", "a")` then `h.write("This is question 4")` then `h.close()`.

questions.prompt: Name the three constructs used when designing an algorithm, and explain how a sequence works.
markPoints: Sequencing
selection
iteration. In a sequence
actions/instructions are carried out in the order they are written
with no instruction skipped
questions.explanation: Model answer: Sequencing, selection, iteration. In a sequence, actions/instructions are carried out in the order they are written, with no instruction skipped.

questions.prompt: What is a syntax error, and give two examples of what might cause one in Python.
markPoints: A syntax error is an error in the code itself
such as missing punctuation/colons
incorrect indentation
misspelled commands (e.g. `prnit`)
questions.explanation: Model answer: A syntax error is an error in the code itself, such as missing punctuation/colons, incorrect indentation, or misspelled commands (e.g. `prnit`).

questions.prompt: What is a logic error, and how does it differ from a syntax error?
markPoints: A logic error occurs when a program runs without crashing but does not produce the expected/intended result
a syntax error stops the program running and produces an error message
questions.explanation: Model answer: A logic error occurs when a program runs without crashing but does not produce the expected/intended result; a syntax error stops the program running and produces an error message.

questions.prompt: Identify the bug in this code, and explain why it produces the wrong output:
markPoints: The statements are in the wrong sequence: multiplying before adding gives x = 4*3+5 = 17, instead of the intended (4+5)*3 = 27 — the order of the statements is the bug
questions.explanation: Model answer: The statements are in the wrong sequence: multiplying before adding gives x = 4*3+5 = 17, instead of the intended (4+5)*3 = 27 — the order of the statements is the bug.
questions.code:
x = 4
x = x * 3
x = x + 5
print(x)

questions.prompt: What is the term for a mistake found and corrected during debugging, and what is the process itself called?
markPoints: The mistake is called a "bug"
the process of finding and fixing it is called debugging
questions.explanation: Model answer: The mistake is called a "bug"; the process of finding and fixing it is called debugging.

questions.prompt: What is IDLE, and what is it used for?
markPoints: IDLE is the Integrated Development Learning Environment included with Python
it helps identify mistakes such as syntax and runtime errors, and has a Debug Control window
questions.explanation: Model answer: IDLE is the Integrated Development Learning Environment included with Python; it helps identify mistakes such as syntax and runtime errors, and has a Debug Control window.

questions.prompt: What is "print debugging" and when might it be used instead of a debugger?
markPoints: Print debugging uses `print()` statements to display text/variable values in the console at points in the code; it is used when a debugger is unavailable, e.g. on small IoT devices
questions.explanation: Model answer: Print debugging uses `print()` statements to display text/variable values in the console at points in the code; it is used when a debugger is unavailable, e.g. on small IoT devices.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between IF, ELIF and ELSE statements in Python.
markPoints: IF evaluates an expression and executes the statement(s) if true
ELIF tests a further condition only if the previous condition(s) were false
ELSE executes for anything not covered by the previous conditions

questions.explanation: Model answer: The IPA allows the patent holder to provide an internet link to a website giving details of the patent number, instead of having to display the patent number itself.

questions.prompt: Which regulations allow employers to monitor employees' electronic communications without needing prior employee consent?
markPoints: The Telecommunications Regulations 2000
questions.explanation: Model answer: The Telecommunications Regulations 2000.

questions.prompt: Identify three reasons an employer may want to monitor electronic communications.
markPoints: identifying criminal activity
checking employees work to required standards
checking correct procedures are followed
investigating allegations of misconduct
checking for mishandling of confidential information
checking systems aren't being abused
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any three of: identifying criminal activity, checking employees work to required standards, checking correct procedures are followed, investigating allegations of misconduct, checking for mishandling of confidential information, checking systems aren't being abused.

questions.prompt: Name three systems that can be used to monitor a workplace or employees.
markPoints: key logging
video/audio surveillance (CCTV)
GPS vehicle tracking
location tracking by access badge
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any three of: key logging, video/audio surveillance (CCTV), GPS vehicle tracking, location tracking by access badge.

questions.prompt: What is a keylogger, and what can it record?
markPoints: A keylogger is software that records every key press (and often mouse clicks/screenshots), including usernames, passwords, emails written and websites visited
questions.explanation: Model answer: A keylogger is software that records every key press (and often mouse clicks/screenshots), including usernames, passwords, emails written and websites visited.

questions.prompt: Under the DPA/GDPR, what restriction applies to CCTV cameras regarding audio recording?
markPoints: CCTV audio must not be recorded, except in exceptional circumstances such as panic buttons in a taxi or monitoring in a private area of a police custody room
questions.explanation: Model answer: CCTV audio must not be recorded, except in exceptional circumstances such as panic buttons in a taxi or monitoring in a private area of a police custody room.

questions.prompt: What must employers do regarding informing employees and the ICO when using CCTV?
markPoints: Employers must inform employees that CCTV is in use (with clear, visible signage) and must inform the ICO that CCTV is being used in the workplace
questions.explanation: Model answer: Employers must inform employees that CCTV is in use (with clear, visible signage) and must inform the ICO that CCTV is being used in the workplace.

questions.prompt: What is a subject access request (SAR), and how does it relate to CCTV footage?
markPoints: A SAR is a request made by a data subject to access personal data held about them
employers must provide CCTV footage if a valid SAR is made
questions.explanation: Model answer: A SAR is a request made by a data subject to access personal data held about them; employers must provide CCTV footage if a valid SAR is made.

questions.prompt: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of GPS vehicle tracking.
markPoints: Advantage: it lets employers track vehicle location for safety, e.g. contacting a driver if a vehicle stops or has broken down. Disadvantage: loss of line of sight (e.g. buildings, tunnels, hills) can cause inconsistent or erratic tracking data
questions.explanation: Model answer: Advantage: it lets employers track vehicle location for safety, e.g. contacting a driver if a vehicle stops or has broken down. Disadvantage: loss of line of sight (e.g. buildings, tunnels, hills) can cause inconsistent or erratic tracking data.

questions.prompt: Why is "secret monitoring" of employees generally illegal in the UK, and what is a rare exception?
markPoints: Data protection legislation makes secret monitoring illegal in most areas (e.g. staff bathrooms)
the rare exception is when there is strong suspicion of serious crime (e.g. drug dealing) taking place in that area
questions.explanation: Model answer: Data protection legislation makes secret monitoring illegal in most areas (e.g. staff bathrooms); the rare exception is when there is strong suspicion of serious crime (e.g. drug dealing) taking place in that area.

questions.prompt: What does Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) protect, and what is one exception to it?
markPoints: Article 8 protects a person's right to respect for their correspondence, family life, home and private life
an exception is covert surveillance for a perceived threat to national security or serious criminal activity
questions.explanation: Model answer: Article 8 protects a person's right to respect for their correspondence, family life, home and private life; an exception is covert surveillance for a perceived threat to national security or serious criminal activity.

questions.prompt: What does the ECPA (Electronic Communications Privacy Act) cover, and which US Act does it include?
markPoints: The ECPA is US legislation protecting phone and electronic communications while being made, in transit, and when stored
it includes the Stored Communications Act (SCA), which covers content of emails/messages and metadata
questions.explanation: Model answer: The ECPA is US legislation protecting phone and electronic communications while being made, in transit, and when stored; it includes the Stored Communications Act (SCA), which covers content of emails/messages and metadata.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the CAN-SPAM Act, and what must unsolicited commercial emails include as a result?
markPoints: CAN-SPAM aims to prevent unsolicited/deceptive commercial email
as a result, such emails must be identified as advertising and must give recipients a way to opt out
questions.explanation: Model answer: CAN-SPAM aims to prevent unsolicited/deceptive commercial email; as a result, such emails must be identified as advertising and must give recipients a way to opt out.

questions.prompt: Name the three main professional bodies connected to digital professionals.
markPoints: The British Computer Society (BCS)
the Institute of Analysts
Programmers (IAP)
the Association for Computer Machinery (ACM)
questions.explanation: Model answer: The British Computer Society (BCS), the Institute of Analysts and Programmers (IAP) and the Association for Computer Machinery (ACM).

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a professional body's code of conduct?
markPoints: A code of conduct provides members with a set of guidelines and principles to follow, defining how they should behave professionally and upholding the philosophy of the body
questions.explanation: Model answer: A code of conduct provides members with a set of guidelines and principles to follow, defining how they should behave professionally and upholding the philosophy of the body.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a code of conduct and a code of practice.
markPoints: A code of conduct is a set of guidelines members are advised to follow, whereas a code of practice makes these guidelines mandatory and must be followed exactly to comply with it
questions.explanation: Model answer: A code of conduct is a set of guidelines members are advised to follow, whereas a code of practice makes these guidelines mandatory and must be followed exactly to comply with it.

questions.prompt: Give two areas that might be covered in a code of practice, beyond a basic code of conduct.
markPoints: professional responsibilities (quality of work, deadlines, confidentiality)
contribution to society
health and safety
security and privacy
and ownership/confidentiality relating to innovation
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any two of: professional responsibilities (quality of work, deadlines, confidentiality), contribution to society, health and safety, security and privacy, and ownership/confidentiality relating to innovation.

questions.prompt: Which UK regulations were created to reduce digital devices going to landfill, and when did they become law?
markPoints: The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Recycling Regulations 2013, which became UK law on 1 January 2014 (updated 1 January 2019)
questions.explanation: Model answer: The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Recycling Regulations 2013, which became UK law on 1 January 2014 (updated 1 January 2019).

questions.prompt: Define "ethics", and name the two main areas of ethical concern relating to digital devices.
markPoints: Ethics are the moral principles or rules that govern a person's attitudes and behaviour
the two main areas of ethical concern for digital devices are privacy of stored data and cyber security
questions.explanation: Model answer: Ethics are the moral principles or rules that govern a person's attitudes and behaviour; the two main areas of ethical concern for digital devices are privacy of stored data and cyber security.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the "digital divide," and name the four (or five) main factors contributing to it.
markPoints: The digital divide is the assumption that everyone has equal access to and ability to use digital devices/the internet
its main factors are wealth, location, specific needs (disabilities), and ability to use new technology
questions.explanation: Model answer: The digital divide is the assumption that everyone has equal access to and ability to use digital devices/the internet; its main factors are wealth, location, specific needs (disabilities), and ability to use new technology.

questions.prompt: What does Article 9 of the UNCRPD (United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities) define?
markPoints: Article 9 of the UNCRPD defines the specific rights of people with disabilities to access digital devices
questions.explanation: Model answer: Article 9 of the UNCRPD defines the specific rights of people with disabilities to access digital devices.

questions.prompt: Give an example of how legal considerations (e.g. DPA, CMA) might be reflected in a code of practice.
markPoints: A code of practice may state that data such as credit card details must be handled in compliance with the DPA and CMA, covering how data is stored, accessed and secured
questions.explanation: Model answer: A code of practice may state that data such as credit card details must be handled in compliance with the DPA and CMA, covering how data is stored, accessed and secured.

questions.prompt: What does ISO stand for, and what is the aim of the organisation?
markPoints: ISO stands for International Organization for Standardization
its aim is to bring together experts to develop voluntary, consensus-based, market-relevant international standards
questions.explanation: Model answer: ISO stands for International Organization for Standardization; its aim is to bring together experts to develop voluntary, consensus-based, market-relevant international standards.

questions.prompt: What is the focus of the ISO 27000 series of standards?
markPoints: The ISO 27000 series focuses on the safety of information assets, including personal, organisational, national security and government data (e.g. held in the cloud)
questions.explanation: Model answer: The ISO 27000 series focuses on the safety of information assets, including personal, organisational, national security and government data (e.g. held in the cloud).

questions.prompt: What does W3C stand for, and who is credited with leading it?
markPoints: W3C stands for the World Wide Web Consortium
it is headed by Tim Berners-Lee (and Jeffrey Jaffe)
questions.explanation: Model answer: W3C stands for the World Wide Web Consortium; it is headed by Tim Berners-Lee (and Jeffrey Jaffe).

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between "the internet" and "the World Wide Web".
markPoints: The internet is the global network of interconnected networks using standardised protocols
the World Wide Web is an information space of resources identified by URIs that runs on top of the internet
questions.explanation: Model answer: The internet is the global network of interconnected networks using standardised protocols; the World Wide Web is an information space of resources identified by URIs that runs on top of the internet.

questions.prompt: Who is credited with inventing the World Wide Web, and what three technologies did they create specifications for?
markPoints: Tim Berners-Lee
he created the first specifications for URLs, HTTP and HTML
questions.explanation: Model answer: Tim Berners-Lee; he created the first specifications for URLs, HTTP and HTML.

questions.prompt: What are WCAG, and what is their overall aim?
markPoints: WCAG are the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, created by W3C, aiming to define a standard for web content accessibility that meets the needs of individuals, organisations and governments worldwide
questions.explanation: Model answer: WCAG are the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, created by W3C, aiming to define a standard for web content accessibility that meets the needs of individuals, organisations and governments worldwide.

questions.prompt: Name the four guiding principles of WCAG 2.1, and briefly explain one of them.
markPoints: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust
e.g. "Perceivable" means information and UI components must be presentable in ways users can perceive with their senses
questions.explanation: Model answer: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust; e.g. "Perceivable" means information and UI components must be presentable in ways users can perceive with their senses.

questions.prompt: What does IETF stand for, and what is its mission?
markPoints: IETF stands for Internet Engineering Task Force
its mission is to make the internet work better by producing high-quality technical documents that influence how people design, use and manage the internet
questions.explanation: Model answer: IETF stands for Internet Engineering Task Force; its mission is to make the internet work better by producing high-quality technical documents that influence how people design, use and manage the internet.

questions.prompt: What is an RFC, and what are the two categories of errors that can be identified in one?
markPoints: An RFC (Request for Comments) is a technical/organisational document issued by the IETF
errors in RFCs are categorised as technical (errors in technical content) or editorial (spelling/grammar/syntax errors not affecting technical meaning)
questions.explanation: Model answer: An RFC (Request for Comments) is a technical/organisational document issued by the IETF; errors in RFCs are categorised as technical (errors in technical content) or editorial (spelling/grammar/syntax errors not affecting technical meaning).

questions.prompt: What is an AUP, and why might an organisation require a signed AUP before granting log-in access?
markPoints: An AUP is an agreement between employers and employees (or a centre and students) setting down rules for using a network, email or the internet
it is required before log-in details are provided so users understand acceptable use
questions.explanation: Model answer: An AUP is an agreement between employers and employees (or a centre and students) setting down rules for using a network, email or the internet; it is required before log-in details are provided so users understand acceptable use.

questions.prompt: Identify three areas that may be covered by the contents of an AUP.
markPoints: monitoring carried out by the employer
non-acceptable activities (e.g. personal email/internet/social media use)
procedures for removable storage devices
and rules for taking/using business devices off-site
questions.explanation: Model answer: Any three of: monitoring carried out by the employer, non-acceptable activities (e.g. personal email/internet/social media use), procedures for removable storage devices, and rules for taking/using business devices off-site.

questions.prompt: Scenario: A retail company is launching a website that will collect customers' names, addresses, phone numbers and email addresses, and wants to email customers about new products. Which piece(s) of legislation must the company comply with regarding storing and using this data, and why?
markPoints: The company must comply with the DPA/GDPR (as it is collecting and storing personal data such as name, address and email) and should also consider the CMA regarding securing the data from unauthorised access
consent/opt-in rules also apply before sending marketing emails
questions.explanation: Model answer: The company must comply with the DPA/GDPR (as it is collecting and storing personal data such as name, address and email) and should also consider the CMA regarding securing the data from unauthorised access; consent/opt-in rules also apply before sending marketing emails.

questions.prompt: Scenario: A company wants to ensure its new website works well for a visually impaired user using a screen reader. Which set of guidelines should the company follow, and which of its principles is most relevant?
markPoints: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines)
the "Perceivable" principle is most relevant, as it requires information and UI components to be presentable in ways users can perceive (e.g. via screen reader-compatible alternative text)
questions.explanation: Model answer: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines); the "Perceivable" principle is most relevant, as it requires information and UI components to be presentable in ways users can perceive (e.g. via screen reader-compatible alternative text).

questions.prompt: Scenario: An employer wants to install hidden cameras in the staff break room without telling employees. Explain why this is likely to be illegal under UK data protection legislation.

simply wanting general oversight of a break room would not meet this exception, and staff have an expectation of privacy in such spaces
